overview: Environmental engineers design systems that protect people and nature: water treatment plants, air pollution controls, waste cleanup and recycling programs. They assess the impact of land use projects, check compliance with rules and work with scientists and planners. O*NET rates knowledge of engineering and technology at 4.95 out of 5 for this job and chemistry at 4.05. A bachelor's degree is required, held by 62% in O*NET data, and 29% hold a master's. The BLS May 2025 median is $107,110 across 38,340 jobs. Site visits sometimes mean working outdoors in all weather.
pay: Environmental engineers earn a median of $107,110, and the top 10% earn $162,220 or more. Louisiana and California have the highest state medians, $130,510 and $130,410, both 22% above the national figure. California also has the most jobs, 4,550, followed by New York with 3,170.

faq.q: How much do environmental engineers make?
faq.a: The BLS May 2025 median is $107,110 a year. The middle half earn between $83,570 and $134,420. Louisiana, California and Oregon ($127,100) pay the most, often in energy, water and consulting work, while Arkansas ($85,280) and West Virginia ($83,200) have the lowest state medians.

faq.q: What degree do you need to be an environmental engineer?
faq.a: A bachelor's degree in environmental, civil or chemical engineering is the usual start. In O*NET data, 62% hold a bachelor's degree and 29% a master's degree. Many earn a Professional Engineer (PE) license after about 4 years of work, which is needed to sign off on public projects.

faq.q: What do environmental engineers do every day?
faq.a: Most days mix design work, data analysis and report writing with site visits and meetings with clients or regulators. O*NET rates reading comprehension, writing, monitoring and speaking at 4 out of 5 for this job, since permits and reports take up much of the work.

faq.q: What jobs are similar to environmental engineer?
faq.a: The closest are Water Resource Specialists (93% match), brownfield redevelopment specialists (89%) and Hydrologists (81%), based on O*NET 31.0. Materials Scientists are an 80% match and earn $117,790, 10% more, according to BLS May 2025 data. Hydrologists earn $96,600, which is 10% less.
